action_criteria.label: Lumbar tap test with opening pressure
action_criteria.rationale: A normal opening pressure with normal CSF and an objective gait response to CSF removal supports probable iNPH and predicts shunt benefit.

action_criteria.label: Post-tap timed gait reassessment
action_criteria.rationale: Repeating the timed measures at 2 and 24 hours after the 38 mL tap separates the part of his gait that responds to CSF removal from the residual spastic myelopathy, which should not change.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]
Do not attribute the new gait and bladder decline to recurrent cervical myelopathy when the spine MRI shows a solid fusion without new compression
Do not withhold shunt referral solely because of the coexisting cervical myelopathy
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 22% in TUG at 24 hours, the DESH-pattern MRI and normal-pressure CSF [Nakajima_2021]

Counsel that shunting is expected to improve the gait, urinary and cognitive changes of iNPH more than the spastic myelopathic features, which will persist, and that the myelopathy continues to need its own rehabilitation and spinal follow-up
Review gabapentin and baclofen as contributors to unsteadiness and cognitive slowing and keep the doses unchanged across the tap test (baclofen is never stopped abruptly)
Falls-prevention measures (physiotherapy, home assessment, walking aid) while awaiting surgery

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no role in a chronic gait and cognitive syndrome without seizures or fluctuating awareness
There is no syncope, palpitation or cardiac question in this gait and cognitive work-up
Echocardiography answers no question in this work-up: there is no cardioembolic event or heart failure
Head CT adds nothing once brain MRI is available, which measures the ventricles, callosal angle and DESH better
Rhythm monitoring has no role without syncope or a suspected arrhythmia
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the iNPH decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the iNPH decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are
Prion, inflammatory and infectious CSF assays answer no question in a chronic afebrile gait syndrome with normal CSF cells

accepted: Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus with concurrent cervical spondylotic myelopathy

differential.diagnosis: Recurrent or adjacent-segment cervical spondylotic myelopathy
differential.key_features: The spine MRI shows a solid C3-C6 fusion with no recurrent or adjacent-segment compression and an unchanged chronic cord signal, and the gait and bladder symptoms improved after CSF removal.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: Deep white matter disease is only Fazekas grade 1 without lacunes, which does not account for the gait disorder or the ventricular enlargement.

differential.diagnosis: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy contributing to gait
differential.key_features: Vibration is reduced to the knees, but brisk reflexes and a magnetic gait that improved after CSF removal are not explained by neuropathy.
No rest tremor or upper-limb bradykinesia; the lower-body gait disorder improved after CSF removal.
Hippocampi are preserved (MTA 1) and the MoCA shows executive and attentional errors with recall improved by cueing rather than an amnestic profile.
Tight high-convexity sulci (DESH) and an acute callosal angle of 82 degrees argue against ventricular enlargement from atrophy.

differential.diagnosis: Secondary communicating hydrocephalus (post-traumatic, post-haemorrhagic or post-meningitic)
differential.key_features: No head injury with haemorrhage, subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis precedes the decline, and MRI shows no haemosiderin.

key_clinical_evidence: Probable iNPH requires insidious onset after age 40, at least 3 to 6 months of progression, no antecedent such as trauma, haemorrhage or meningitis, and a gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms [Relkin_2005]

Imaging criterion: Evans index greater than 0.3 without obstruction, with supportive features (DESH, acute callosal angle, temporal horn enlargement); here Evans 0.36, DESH, callosal angle 82 degrees [Relkin_2005] [Nakajima_2021]

Normal opening pressure (17 cmH2O) with normal CSF content; after a 30 to 50 mL tap [Nakajima_2021], TUG improved 22% at 24 hours, above the 10% improvement commonly used as a positive threshold (no guideline sets a single cut-off)
Tap-test sensitivity is 26% to 61% with PPV 73% to 100%, so a positive tap supports shunt referral while a negative one would not exclude it [Marmarou_2005]
The cervical spine MRI shows a solid fusion without new compression, so the second deterioration is not explained by recurrent myelopathy; the residual spasticity will not respond to a shunt

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The spine MRI shows a solid fusion without new compression and the gait and bladder decline improved after CSF removal, so the second deterioration is iNPH superimposed on stable residual myelopathy.
red_herrings.data_point: Severe cervical spondylotic myelopathy (C3-C6, status post anterior cervical discectomy and fusion 3 years ago, incomplete functional recovery)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Gait and bladder deterioration is attributed to recurrent cervical myelopathy

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Diabetic neuropathy may explain the reduced vibration sense, but not a magnetic, short-stepped gait with brisk reflexes that improves after CSF removal.
red_herrings.data_point: Reduced vibration bilateral lower extremities to knees, with type 2 diabetes mellitus on metformin
red_herrings.intended_effect: Gait disturbance is attributed to diabetic peripheral neuropathy

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]
The timed gait is repeated after the tap, at 2 to 24 hours, so that its change from the baseline measures the response to CSF removal [Nakajima_2021]

patient.history_present_illness: A 78-year-old retired civil engineer with severe cervical spondylotic myelopathy (C3-C6 fusion 3 years ago with incomplete recovery) was admitted for neurological evaluation of progressive gait deterioration and new urinary incontinence that his spinal surgeon feels is disproportionate to his cervical disease. Three years ago he underwent C3-C6 anterior cervical discectomy and fusion for severe cervical myelopathy causing bilateral arm weakness, gait ataxia, and hyperreflexia. His post-operative course was characterized by partial motor recovery: he remained ambulatory with a cane and had acceptable bladder control. Over the past 18 months he has had a second deterioration. His gait has become wider-based and slower, with a magnetic quality that his physical therapist describes as 'not just myelopathy.' He has had five falls. Urinary urgency and incontinence appeared 12 months ago and have been attributed to his myelopathy, but his spinal surgeon notes the timing and severity seem beyond the expected myelopathy contribution. Cognitive decline over 8 months has also been noted; his daughter describes increased forgetfulness and slowed thinking. A head CT obtained after a fall 6 months ago at an outside facility was reported as showing enlarged ventricles; the images are not available.
